title: Check {name}'s skin and coat
why: Noticing new redness, flakes or hair loss early gives you time to plan a routine vet question.

why: Regular checks help you notice a chipped tooth or mouth change before the next estimate is a surprise.

title: Do an at-home weigh-in
why: A simple weight log gives your veterinarian useful context at the next wellness exam.

title: Confirm the microchip contact details
why: Current registration details protect the value of the microchip you already paid for.

title: Check when the next wellness visit is due
why: Planning ahead turns a routine exam into a budget line instead of a surprise bill.

title: Look at {name}'s eyes for redness or discharge
why: Red, cloudy or weepy eyes are a common reason for a sick visit. Spotting the change early lets you call the vet before it gets worse.

title: Wash {name}'s water bowl and refill it
why: Fresh water encourages drinking, and a daily wash stops slime from building up inside the bowl.

title: Measure {name}'s meals with a cup or kitchen scale
why: US vets rated 59% of dogs and 61% of cats overweight or obese in 2022. Measuring every meal is one of the easiest ways to keep weight, and food spending, in check.

title: Gently touch {name}'s paws, ears and mouth, then give a treat
why: AAHA suggests short, positive handling sessions at home so exams, nail trims and tooth checks feel calm instead of scary.

title: Check {name}'s paws and nails
why: Cracked pads, stuck burrs and overgrown nails are easy to catch at home and painful if they are missed.

title: Brush {name}'s coat for five minutes
why: Brushing removes loose hair and lets you feel for new lumps, scabs or fleas while they are still small.

title: Take {name} on a 20-minute sniff walk
why: A walk with time to sniff burns calories and tires the brain, which helps with both weight and boredom behaviors.

title: Serve one of {name}'s meals in a puzzle toy or snuffle mat
why: Working for food slows down fast eaters and adds mental exercise without adding calories.

title: Do a 5-minute training session with {name}
why: AAHA recommends short, fun training sessions to keep skills fresh and build confidence for vet visits.

title: Scoop {name}'s litter box and look for changes
why: Cat vets advise scooping at least once a day. Bigger, more or fewer clumps than usual can be an early sign of a urinary or kidney problem worth asking the vet about.

title: Play with {name} using a wand toy for 10 minutes
why: Indoor cats still need to stalk and pounce. A short daily play session burns calories and lowers stress.

title: Serve part of {name}'s food in a food puzzle
why: The American Association of Feline Practitioners recommends puzzle feeders and small, frequent meals to reduce boredom, begging and weight gain.

title: Leave a treat in {name}'s carrier
why: AAHA advises keeping the carrier out all the time so it stops meaning 'vet trip'. A relaxed cat makes yearly checkups much easier to keep up with.

title: Wash {name}'s bed and blankets
why: A hot wash removes hair, dander and flea eggs that collect where pets sleep.

title: Empty and wash {name}'s litter box
why: Scooping leaves some waste behind. Vets suggest washing the box with mild soap every one to four weeks; a clean box helps prevent accidents around the house.
